findings.quote: statistically significant group differences after 17 ( F (1,13) = 4.65; P < 0.05

consequence.explanation: One of the two per-experiment ANCOVAs the paper calls 'statistically significant group differences' does not reach the alpha = 0.05 it is claimed against; this is a load-bearing step in the dose-response argument.

findings.notes: The upper tail of F is the only tail F has, so no one-tailed reading rescues this. The whole rounding interval implied by the printed F (4.645 to 4.655) sits above 0.05, so the discrepancy is not a rounding artefact. The innocent explanations are (a) the authors rounded 0.0504 down to 'P < 0.05' by eye, or (b) the printed F is itself rounded from a computation whose unrounded value they tested. Note that recalc_stat_to_p returned 'consistent' for this row: that tool is DIRECTIONAL and takes reported_p = 0.05 as an equality, so it only flags a p BELOW the achievable interval. The finding rests on the printed operator 'P < 0.05', which neither tool accepts as an argument.

severity_source.note: The tool returned `consistent`; this finding records `suspicious`. A reason is stated in the finding.

findings.quote: revealed a trend for group differences after 12 days ( F (1,19) = 1.93; P = 0.09

computed.method: for each ANCOVA, divide the p computed by recalc_f_to_p by 2 and compare with what the paper printed

inputs.source_values: the three computed p-values returned by recalc_f_to_p for F(1,19)=1.93, F(1,13)=4.65 and F(1,12)=4.53

consequence.explanation: If the three ANCOVA p-values were obtained by halving, then the paper's claim of 'statistically significant group differences after 17 and 19 training days' -- the per-experiment evidence for the dose-response conclusion in the abstract -- rests on a halving that the F distribution does not license.

findings.notes: The 12-day row pins the factor exactly (0.181 / 0.09 = 2.01), and halving the other two computed p-values gives 0.025 and 0.027, both of which would be reported as 'P < 0.05'. A single coherent explanation covers all three: one-tailed p-values. The F distribution has no one-tailed variant -- its p is an upper tail by construction -- so halving is not a recognised convention here, though it is a recognised convention for a directional t-test and a plausible route if the authors converted from a t. This is an inference across three tool results rather than a single computation, and it is capped at `suspicious` accordingly. No registered tool tests a family of p-values for a common scaling factor.

findings.location: Results, footnote on the four training functions

consequence.explanation: The four regression F-tests that establish 'an impressive learning curve for the training task in all four experiments' are fitted to roughly twice as many observations as the reported trained sample can supply under the standard reading of the residual df.

findings.notes: THE MODELLING ASSUMPTION IS DOING THE WORK AND MUST BE STATED: this reads df2 as n_observations - 2, the residual df of a simple linear regression of n-back level on session number, which is what 'the specific training gain was well explained by a linear function' most naturally describes. Under that reading each of the four groups independently implies exactly 17 participants -- an identical figure across four groups the paper describes as differently sized (16, 22, 16, 15 combined trained plus control) -- and 4 x 17 = 68 against 34 analysed trained participants. The cleanest innocent explanation is that each participant contributed TWO data points per session, one per modality stream, which would halve the implied counts; but that requires exactly 8.5 participants in every one of the four groups, which is not possible, so it does not resolve the discrepancy. Other innocent routes: the regression may have been fitted at block level rather than session level, or may include terms whose df I cannot see. Because the finding rests on an assumed model rather than a stated one, it is capped at `suspicious` and should not be read as an impossibility.

findings.quote: was substantially superior ( t (33) = 5.53; P < 0.001; Cohen's d = 0.65)

computed.method: compare each printed d with the paired-samples d_z implied by its own t and n, d_z = t / sqrt(n)

consequence.explanation: No claim is affected: the two effect sizes are mutually consistent under a single standardiser, so neither appears mistyped.

findings.notes: Neither printed d equals t/sqrt(n), but both fall short of it by nearly the same factor (0.69 and 0.71), which is the signature of a legitimate alternative standardiser -- d computed against the pooled pre/post SD rather than the SD of the difference scores. That conversion factor corresponds to a pre-post correlation of roughly 0.75, an unremarkable value for a repeated administration of a matrices test. I record this as CONSISTENT rather than as an anomaly: the check ran and found the two values coherent with each other. It cannot be pushed further because the paper prints the Gf means and SDs only in Figure 3, so check_effect_plausibility could not be given group statistics to test the printed d against.
findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies for the d_z conversion: recalc_within_subjects_t is MCP-only and recovers a correlation rather than a d, and the group means and SDs it would need are printed only in Figure 3.

reported.correction_stated_by_authors: none for this family; Gabriel's procedure is used only for the four post-hoc contrasts among training groups

inputs.family_label: Primary Gf-transfer and dose-response tests on the same 69 participants

consequence.explanation: Of four results significant at uncorrected alpha, two survive every correction method; the two lost are the control-group retest t-test and the group x test-session interaction that the paper cites as confirming the transfer effect.

findings.notes: The p-values passed here are the EXACT values recomputed by recalc_f_to_p and recalc_stat_to_p, not the paper's printed thresholds -- six of the seven are printed as bounds, which multiplicity_report would otherwise drop, leaving the family uncheckable. Family definition is a judgement: these seven tests bear on one hypothesis in one pooled sample, which is the standard case for family-wise control. A reader who regards the four experiments as separate studies would define smaller families and lose fewer claims. Uncorrected testing is ordinary in this literature and this is arithmetic about the numbers, not an allegation. All four survivors and casualties are unchanged whichever of the four correction methods is used, which is unusual and makes the bound tight.

findings.quote: There was an effect of training ( F (1,68) = 6.38; P < 0.05

consequence.explanation: Affects the two median-split analyses supporting the claim that the training benefit is independent of initial Gf; it does not bear on the primary transfer or dose-response claims.

findings.notes: This is a cross-reference contradiction, not a calculation. The paper analyses 69 participants (34 trained plus 35 control) and uses error df 67 for its two-group comparisons on that sample, which is what N minus 2 gives. The two median-split analyses in this paragraph both report error df 68, which corresponds to N = 70 -- the total BEFORE the one participant who failed to complete training was discarded. A 2 (training) x 2 (performance group) between-subjects model on 69 participants would give error df 65, not 68, so neither the stated analysed N nor the described design produces 68 under a standard reading. The likeliest innocent explanation is that the excluded participant's pretest data was retained for these particular analyses; the paper does not say so.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: this is a comparison between the degrees of freedom printed in two places and the sample size stated in Methods, not an arithmetic result.

consequence.explanation: These four null results support the Discussion claims that the training 'proved to be useful for all participants and had no adverse effects for participants with high initial working memory capacity' and that the gain is unrelated to initial ability -- conclusions that cannot be evaluated without knowing what effects the data still permit.

findings.notes: absence_of_evidence is the right check and could not be run on any of the four: it requires a confidence interval, or a coefficient with its standard error, and the paper prints only bounds on F with no effect size, no interval, and in one case no df. 'Not significant' is not 'no effect', and at these sample sizes (n as low as 15 per experiment) the intervals around these nulls would be wide. This is a reporting gap recorded as indeterminate, not an anomaly in the numbers. The paper is also explicitly candid about one of them, noting that 'numerically the lowGf participants showed somewhat larger gains'.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: absence_of_evidence requires an interval or a coefficient with its standard error, and the paper prints neither for any of these four null claims.

findings.notes: The paper contains no tables at all; the PDF extraction returned zero. This is the single largest coverage limit on this review. With the group means, SDs and ns, GRIM and GRIMMER would apply directly (the Gf score is a count of correct solutions, an integer), recalc_independent_t and rivets_independent_t could test the reported t values against the group statistics, and check_effect_plausibility could test the printed Cohen's d for internal consistency. None of that was possible. Values read off the bars would carry figure_pixels provenance and are barred from the exact-arithmetic family, so digitising them would not recover these checks.

findings.notes: The paper states two hypotheses in advance (transfer, and dose-dependence) and both are treated as confirmatory in this review's anatomy on the strength of the abstract, but no registration or protocol is cited, so the distinction between confirmatory and exploratory rests on the paper's own framing. This is unremarkable for a 2008 publication -- preregistration was not a norm in this field at the time -- and is recorded for completeness rather than as a criticism. No data-availability statement is present and no supplementary files accompany the article.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: this is a reading of the paper's front matter.

unchecked.location: Figure 3a and 3b -- fluid intelligence means, gain scores and standard errors
unchecked.reason: The paper contains no tables and prints no Gf means or SDs in the text; extract_pdf returned zero tables. The outcome data exist only as bars. Values read off the marks would carry figure_pixels provenance, which is barred from GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE and DEBIT, so digitising them would not restore the checks that matter. This blocks recalc_independent_t, rivets_independent_t, grim_check, grimmer_check and the internal-consistency form of check_effect_plausibility.

unchecked.location: Figure 2 -- mean n-back level per session for each training group
unchecked.reason: The per-session means underlying the four regression F-tests in the footnote appear only in this line plot. Without them the training functions cannot be refitted, so the residual-df anomaly could only be approached through the printed df, not through the data.

unchecked.location: Results, paragraph 2 -- Gabriel post-hoc contrasts (8 vs 17, 8 vs 19, 12 vs 19, 12 vs 17 days)
unchecked.reason: Reported as p-values alone with no test statistic, no df and no group means. Nothing can be recomputed. multiplicity_report was deliberately NOT run on these: Gabriel's procedure already applies a correction, and the paper says so, so adding a second correction would double-count.

unchecked.location: Results, paragraphs 3-5 -- the four null claims (F < 1, F(1,68) < 0.3, F(1,52) < 0.1, and 'both groups improved equally' on reading span)
unchecked.reason: absence_of_evidence requires a confidence interval or a coefficient with its standard error; the paper prints only bounds on F. The largest effect each null still permits therefore cannot be stated.

unchecked.location: Materials and Methods -- r = 0.95 correlation between speeded and non-speeded test versions
unchecked.reason: Quoted from reference 37 rather than measured in this study, and printed with no n and no interval. check_estimate_ci needs an interval and check_statistic_bounds would only confirm that 0.95 lies inside [-1, 1], which establishes nothing.

unchecked.location: Whole paper -- baseline comparability of trained and control groups
unchecked.reason: csf_test and bayesian_table1_dispersion were not run because the paper reports no baseline characteristics table. Only pooled age (25.6, SD 3.3) and sex (36 of 70 female) are given, for the whole sample rather than by group, so there are no baseline p-values or group-wise rows to test for excess similarity. Note also that allocation was not randomised -- participants were assigned to training or control -- so the Carlisle family would not apply even if a table existed.

unchecked.location: Whole paper -- duplication checks across tables
unchecked.reason: detect_duplication requires two or more blocks of means and SDs. The paper reports none, so there is nothing to compare within or across.
No supplementary files accompany this article in the supplied directory. This is 'not provided', not 'present but unreadable'.

unchecked.location: Results, paragraph 2 -- Cohen's d = 0.25 and d = 0.65 tested against the group statistics
unchecked.reason: check_effect_plausibility can test a printed d against the means, SDs and ns that produced it, which is the check that catches a mistyped effect size. Those group statistics appear only in Figure 3, so only the weaker consistency check against t and n was possible (recorded as the reported_d_vs_t_and_n finding).

unchecked.location: Design sensitivity (mde_80) for the omnibus and repeated-measures tests
unchecked.reason: required_n covers two-sample t, one-way ANOVA, correlation, chi-square and two-proportion designs. MDE was computed for the two-group comparisons (d = 0.68 at n = 35 per group; d = 1.45 at roughly n = 9 per group in the individual experiments) but not for the group x session interaction or the ANCOVAs, whose sensitivity depends on the pre-post correlation, which the paper does not report.
